<action type="say">
First, let’s stop the damage as much as possible right now:

1. Stop the water:
   - Look behind or near the toilet for the shutoff valve (usually an oval or round handle on the wall or floor line).
   - Turn it clockwise until it stops. If you can’t find it, take the tank lid off and lift the float up with your hand to stop water entering the tank.

2. Prevent electrical danger:
   - If water is near any outlets, power strips, or appliances, do NOT touch them.
   - If you can safely do it without walking through water, turn off power to that bathroom from your breaker panel.

3. Contain the water:
   - Use towels, rags, or a mop to keep water from spreading to other rooms or reaching wood floors or downstairs ceilings.
   - If there’s a floor drain, try to direct water toward it.

I can get you an emergency plumber right away. I just need:

1) The address (or at least city + ZIP code) where you need service  
2) Whether the water is still actively coming out, or just what’s already on the floor  
3) A phone number the plumber can reach you on  

Once you send that, I’ll search for emergency plumbers in your area and move to get someone out ASAP.</action>

Since it’s an apartment and there’s building management, they should be your first call now.

Here’s what to do:

1) Contact building management immediately  
- Call the management office number; if it’s after hours, there’s usually an emergency or maintenance line in your lease, on posted notices near the lobby/mailboxes, or on their website.  
- When you reach them, say:  
  “My toilet overflowed but I’ve shut off the water at the valve. There’s water on the bathroom floor at [your unit number] and I’m concerned about water damage. I need emergency maintenance or a plumber as soon as possible.”  
- Ask: “Do you have an on-call maintenance person or plumber, and what’s the expected response time?”

2) Document the situation (takes 2–3 minutes)  
- Take clear photos of:
  - The bathroom floor and any visible standing water  
  - Any areas where water might have spread (hallway, carpet, baseboards, ceiling below if visible)  
- Note the time the overflow happened and the time you shut the water off; this can help if there are any damage or responsibility questions later.

3) While you wait for maintenance  
- Keep soaking up as much water as you can with towels and wringing them into the tub or sink.  
- If you have a fan, point it toward the wet area to start drying.  
- Don’t use or flush that toilet until maintenance/plumbing has checked it.

Given it’s 8:20 p.m. and maintenance is often slow, I’d treat this as urgent, especially if this is your only bathroom or water spread beyond the bathroom.

Here’s how to handle it:

1) Call the building’s emergency/after-hours maintenance line now  
- Use the emergency number from your lease, lobby, or building website (if there is one), not the “normal hours” office line.  
- Say something like:  
  “My toilet overflowed in unit [your unit #]. I’ve turned off the water at the valve, but there was enough water that I’m worried about damage and possible leaks to other units. I need someone out tonight, please.”  
- Ask specifically:  
  - “Is this being treated as an emergency or a routine ticket?”  
  - “What’s the expected response time tonight?”

2) Decide about calling an outside 24/7 plumber  
If they say they won’t come until tomorrow, and either (a) you only have this one toilet or (b) there was a lot of water:

- Ask management:  
  “If I call a licensed 24/7 plumber myself tonight to stop any further damage, will the building cover or reimburse the cost?”  
- Note down: who you spoke with, the time, and exactly what they said.  
- If they won’t cover it and you still call a plumber, be aware you may be paying out-of-pocket, but you’re also limiting possible damage and hassle.

If you do call a 24/7 plumber:
- Search “24 hour emergency plumber 78701” and pick a well-rated one.  
- Tell them: it’s an apartment, you’ve shut the valve off, the toilet overflowed, water’s on the floor but not actively running.

3) While you’re waiting  
- Keep soaking up as much water as you can with towels; wring them into the tub or sink and re-use them.  
- Run a fan and leave the bathroom door open (if possible) to help it dry.  
- Don’t use or flush that toilet until a professional or maintenance says it’s okay.

Do you have another working bathroom in the apartment, or is this your only one? That will help me suggest how hard to push for immediate help vs. first thing in the morning.</action>
